name: Al-Sayyid Bedouin Sign Language
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: sign language (ABSL); no description of word stress found; ABSL literature covers sign prosody, not word stress

sources.citation: Sandler, Wendy, Irit Meir, Svetlana Dachkovsky, Carol Padden & Mark Aronoff. 2011. The emergence of complexity in prosody and syntax. Lingua 121(13): 2014-2033. doi:10.1016/j.lingua.2011.05.007 (PMC author manuscript PMC3476057)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: The one dedicated ABSL prosody study; fn. 2: 'We omit the prosodic property of stress from the present discussion.' Describes only Intonational-Phrase boundary cues (holds, pauses, reiteration, slowing/enlargement of the final sign, facial intonation); §4.3 says there was 'little evidence for lower prosodic levels such as phonological phrases' in the ABSL corpus. Prosodic-word/syllable/stress facts stated only for ISL, not ABSL.

sources.citation: Sandler, Wendy. 2010. Prosody and syntax in sign languages. Transactions of the Philological Society 108(3): 298-328. doi:10.1111/j.1467-968X.2010.01242.x (PMC3250094)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Fn. 10: 'Little is said here about stress/prominence. The reader is referred to Wilbur (1999), Nespor & Sandler (1999), van der Kooij, Crasborn, & Emmerik (2006), and Sandler (to appear a)'. Stress/prominence discussion concerns ISL and ASL (IP-final prominence; ASL compound stress on second member per Klima & Bellugi); §9 on ABSL covers only pauses, head position, facial expression at constituent boundaries.

sources.citation: Sandler, Wendy, Mark Aronoff, Irit Meir & Carol Padden. 2011. The gradual emergence of phonological form in a new language. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 29(2): 503-543. doi:10.1007/s11049-011-9128-2 (PMC3250231)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: No statement on stress (the only 'stress' tokens are the verb 'we stress' and an English example 'unstressed schwa'). §3: 'Prosodic organization is also evident in ABSL. Even the first generation of signers used rhythmic cues to signal the ends of utterances.' Argues ABSL lacks a fully developed sublexical phonology (no minimal pairs, high sublexical variation).
